entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Yale University, founded in 1701 in New Haven, Connecticut, is the third-oldest university in the United States and one of the most prestigious in the world. With 65 Nobel laureates, 5 US presidents, and the country's second-largest university endowment ($41 billion), Yale has been central to American law, politics, and arts for three centuries, producing more US Supreme Court Justices than any other law school.

Founded by Congregationalist ministers as the Collegiate School of Connecticut, then renamed after benefactor Elihu Yale in 1718, the university evolved from a strictly religious institution to a comprehensive research university. Yale's residential college system, adopted from Oxford and Cambridge in 1933, created a distinctive undergraduate culture. The Yale Law School and its Federalist Society affiliates have profoundly shaped American constitutional law for decades.

Yale's contributions to arts and culture are distinctive: the Yale School of Drama, founded in 1924, has trained generations of American theater and film talent including Meryl Streep, Jodie Foster, and Paul Newman; the Yale School of Music has produced major American composers. Yale's Beinecke Rare Book Library, one of the largest buildings in the world devoted to rare books, houses original manuscripts including Gutenberg Bibles and the controversial Voynich Manuscript. Skull and Bones, the most famous secret society in America, was founded at Yale.
